description: Exp3 round 3 MAP tests of single changes to upward_count_start_boundary; which cues help and which do nothing
metadata:
  type: project
---
Exp3 round 3 (2026-10-18), incumbent upward_count_start_boundary MAP ll −4642.8. Fitted weights: size w≈0.69 per 100 units (weak), graded-factor w≈0.005 (factor similarity basically unused).

name: exp3-r3-residual-scan
description: Exp3 round 3 MAP residual scan of upward_count_start_boundary — which single additions gain (even rule ~9 nats) and which do nothing
metadata:
  type: project
---
Exp3 round 3 (2026-10-18), MAP log-lik of the incumbent upward_count_start_boundary = -4642.8. Single additions tested:

name: leading-digit-similarity-gain
description: Exp3 r3 — adding a leading-digit match dimension to the best model gains ~12.6 nats at MAP
metadata:
  type: project
---
In experiment3 round 3 (2026-10-18), a MAP fit of upward_count_start_boundary showed that targets sharing their first written digit with the examples were under-predicted. ---
name: order-effects-exhausted
description: Exp3 r3 MAP screen — order mechanisms beyond the upward start boundary gain at most ~2 nats
metadata:
  type: project
---
On 2026-10-18 (exp3 round 3) I MAP-fit upward_count_start_boundary (ll −4642.8) and tested order variants. First-example primacy boost gained 2.0 nats (submitted as primacy_recency_serial_position; retention went 0.91→0.77, primacy 0.5). Rehearsal weighting gained 1.7. Coherence from last-anchored pairs gained 1.3. Continuing the last step forward gained 1–1.7. A first- or last-anchored partial span, and successive-pair or first-anchored coherence, gained nothing or lost fit. The largest remaining misfit is set-level (e.g. 63,67, 53,47,41 and 3,33,99 are over-predicted; 31,19,49,100 is under-predicted), not order.
**Why:** this saves re-screening order effects in later rounds.
**How to apply:** for order-themed briefs, expect small gains. Look for bigger wins in set-level structure. Builds on [[residual-ascending-below-start]]. The scripts are in iter_3/candidate_0/scratch (fit.py and varA–K).
---
name: residual-ascending-below-start
description: Exp3 round 2 MAP residual finding — targets below the first example of ascending sets are over-predicted by the best model
metadata:
  type: project
---
In experiment3 round 2 (2026-10-18) a MAP fit of saturating_criterion_relaxation showed that targets below the first example of sets whose last example is larger than the first were over-predicted by about 0.1. Adding one all-or-none logit penalty for those targets improved the MAP log-likelihood by about 28 nats (−4671 to −4643). The symmetric "behind the start" version gained only about 6, and a graded version about 19. Targets 1 and 2 are also over-predicted by about 0.11 overall. This became candidate upward_count_start_boundary.
**Why:** a quick MAP fit plus grouped residuals (scratch/resid.py) finds targeted single mechanisms much faster than reading the critique alone.
**How to apply:** before proposing a candidate, MAP-fit the incumbent and group residuals by set and target structure.

Round 3 (2026-10-18): grafting the same penalty onto sample_size_neglect_range_inference raised its MAP log-likelihood from −4667 to −4639, about 4 better than the incumbent (−4643). The penalty fit at about 0.63 in both models, so it is roughly additive with range inference. This became candidate sample_size_neglect_upward_start.

# Critique of `zigzag_breadth_sequence_exemplar`

2 of 8 evaluated test statistics show a significant discrepancy (p ≤ 0.05), over 1000 posterior-predictive replicates.

## Significant discrepancies (a better model should address these)

Raw two-sided p shown with a Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-adjusted q across this round's statistics. Prioritise discrepancies that survive the FDR (`q ≤ alpha`); a raw-only hit may be one of several screened at once.
- **small_vs_large_region_gap** — Among targets outside the span by a linear gap of 5-40, yes-rate when the nearest example is <=20 minus when the nearest example is >=60; observed < null means people compress large numbers (log-like magnitude) so equal linear gaps matter more among small numbers, which the linear-distance model fails to produce. (observed -0.0584 vs null mean 0.0285, z=-2.94, p=0.00999, q=0.0719)
- **exact_example_target_yes** — Yes-rate on trials whose target is one of the shown examples, minus yes-rate on targets within 1-3 of the nearest example; observed > null means people treat a repeated example as near-certainly produced far more than nearby numbers, and the model under-produces this boost. (observed 0.371 vs null mean 0.304, z=2.44, p=0.018, q=0.0719)

"""Leading-digit string similarity exemplar model.

Refinement of upward_count_start_boundary (all else unchanged). The single
change: people also compare numbers as written digit strings by their leading
digit. A target whose first written digit matches an example's (34 after 31
or 3) feels more similar to that example, all-or-none, with attention to this
match stretched when the examples share a leading digit, so targets sharing
the examples' leading digit are endorsed more than numerical distance alone
predicts.
"""
import math
from functools import reduce

import numpy as np
import pymc as pm
import pytensor.tensor as pt

MAXK = 4
NDIM = 5  # magnitude, final digit, parity, graded shared factor, leading digit
SESSION_LEN = 450.0


def _factor_mismatch(t, x):
    m = min(t, x)
    if m <= 1:
        return 0.0
    return 1.0 - math.log(math.gcd(t, x)) / math.log(m)


def prepare_observed(rows):
    n = len(rows)
    mism = np.ones((n, NDIM, MAXK))
    coh = np.zeros((n, NDIM))
    lag = np.zeros((n, MAXK))
    mask = np.zeros((n, MAXK))
    rule = np.zeros(n)
    digit_rule = np.zeros(n)
    position = np.zeros(n)
    ahead = np.zeros(n)
    below_start = np.zeros(n)
    disorder = np.zeros(n)
    is_example = np.zeros(n)
    rating = np.zeros(n, dtype="int64")
    cache = {}
    for r, row in enumerate(rows):
        s = str(row["number_set"])
        ex = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")][:MAXK]
        t = int(row["target"])
        k = len(ex)
        if s not in cache:
            pairs = [(ex[i], ex[j]) for i in range(k) for j in range(i + 1, k)]
            c = np.zeros(NDIM)
            if pairs:
                c[0] = np.mean([max(0.0, 1.0 - abs(a - b) / 50.0) for a, b in pairs])
                c[1] = np.mean([a % 10 == b % 10 for a, b in pairs])
                c[2] = np.mean([a % 2 == b % 2 for a, b in pairs])
                c[3] = np.mean([1.0 - _factor_mismatch(a, b) for a, b in pairs])
                c[4] = np.mean([str(a)[0] == str(b)[0] for a, b in pairs])
            g = reduce(math.gcd, ex) if k >= 2 else 0
            d = ex[0] % 10 if k >= 2 and len({x % 10 for x in ex}) == 1 else -1
            cache[s] = (c, g, d)

        coh[r] = c
        is_example[r] = 1.0 if t in ex else 0.0
        if g >= 3:

        # the start, 0 inside the span or with no direction (one example).
        travel = (ex[-1] > ex[0]) - (ex[-1] < ex[0])
        out = (t > max(ex)) - (t < min(ex))
        ahead[r] = float(travel * out)
        # Below the starting point of an upward-counting sequence (the change).
        below_start[r] = 1.0 if (travel > 0 and t < ex[0]) else 0.0
        # Share of direction reversals between successive steps in shown
        # order (0 monotone, 1 full zigzag), centred; 0 with fewer than 3.

            mism[r, 1, i] = 0.0 if t % 10 == x % 10 else 1.0
            mism[r, 2, i] = 0.0 if t % 2 == x % 2 else 1.0
            mism[r, 3, i] = _factor_mismatch(t, x)
            # Leading written digit match (the change).
            mism[r, 4, i] = 0.0 if str(t)[0] == str(x)[0] else 1.0
            lag[r, i] = k - 1 - i
            mask[r, i] = 1.0
        ti = row.get("trial_index")
        if ti is not None and str(ti).strip() != "":
            position[r] = min(max(float(ti), 0.0), SESSION_LEN) / SESSION_LEN
        rv = row.get("rating")
        rating[r] = int(float(rv)) if rv is not None and str(rv).strip() != "" else 0
    return {"mismatch": mism, "coherence": coh, "lag": lag, "ex_mask": mask,
            "rule_evidence": rule, "digit_rule_evidence": digit_rule,
            "session_position": position, "ahead": ahead, "below_start": below_start,
            "disorder": disorder, "is_example": is_example, "rating": rating}

    ahead = pm.Data("ahead", np.zeros(1))
    below_start = pm.Data("below_start", np.zeros(1))
    disorder = pm.Data("disorder", np.zeros(1))
    is_example = pm.Data("is_example", np.zeros(1))

    tuning = pm.HalfNormal("tuning", sigma=2.0, shape=NDIM)
    retention = pm.Beta("retention", alpha=2.0, beta=2.0)
    bias = pm.Normal("bias", mu=-1.0, sigma=2.0)
    gain = pm.HalfNormal("gain", sigma=5.0)
    rule_weight = pm.HalfNormal("rule_weight", sigma=1.0)
    digit_rule_weight = pm.HalfNormal("digit_rule_weight", sigma=1.0)
    # How far the yes-criterion relaxes from session start to end.
    criterion_drift = pm.Normal("criterion_drift", mu=0.0, sigma=1.0)
    # Time constant of the relaxation, as a share of the session:
    # small = fast early relaxation then plateau; large = nearly linear.
    relax_tau = pm.Beta("relax_tau", alpha=2.0, beta=4.0)
    relax_shape = ((1.0 - pt.exp(-session_position / relax_tau))
                   / (1.0 - pt.exp(-1.0 / relax_tau)))
    # Evidence from the "fixed list of these numbers" concept.
    list_weight = pm.HalfNormal("list_weight", sigma=2.0)

    # Evidence against numbers below an upward sequence's start (the change).
    start_penalty = pm.HalfNormal("start_penalty", sigma=2.0)

    # Momentum: shrinks size mismatch ahead of the sequence, stretches it behind.
    momentum = pm.Normal("momentum", mu=0.0, sigma=1.0)
    # Zigzag: a disorderly sequence shrinks the size mismatch.
    zigzag_sensitivity = pm.Normal("zigzag_sensitivity", mu=0.0, sigma=1.0)
    size_scale = pt.exp(-momentum * ahead - zigzag_sensitivity * disorder)
    mismatch = pt.set_subtensor(
        mismatch[:, 0, :], mismatch[:, 0, :] * size_scale[:, None])

    attn = w_base[None, :] * pt.exp(tuning[None, :] * coherence)
    dist = pt.sum(attn[:, :, None] * mismatch, axis=1)
    sim = pt.exp(-dist)
    mem = ex_mask * pt.exp(lag * pt.log(retention))
    mem = mem / pt.sum(mem, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    familiarity = pt.sum(mem * sim, axis=1)

    logit = (bias + criterion_drift * relax_shape + gain * familiarity
             + rule_weight * rule_evidence
             + digit_rule_weight * digit_rule_evidence
             + list_weight * is_example
             - start_penalty * below_start)
    p_yes = pm.Deterministic(
        "p_yes", pt.clip(pm.math.sigmoid(logit), 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6))

    rating = pm.Data("rating", np.zeros(1, dtype="int64"))
    pm.Bernoulli("response", p=p_yes, observed=rating)

# name: set_level_yes_rate_dispersion
# description: Standard deviation across example sets with 40+ rows of each set's overall yes-rate; observed > null means people treat some sets as broad and others as narrow more strongly than the model does (model compresses set-level differences), observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    g = df.groupby("number_set")["rating"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    g = g[g["size"] >= 40]
    if len(g) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(g["mean"].std())

cat << 'EOF' > log_magnitude_region_gap.py
# name: log_magnitude_region_gap
# description: Among out-of-span targets 5-40 (linear) from the nearest span edge, yes-rate when that nearest edge is <=20 minus when it is >=60; observed < null means equal linear gaps hurt more among small numbers (log-like magnitude compression), which the model's linear size distance under-produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    mn = ex.min(axis=1).values; mx = ex.max(axis=1).values
    below = t < mn; above = t > mx
    gap = np.where(below, mn - t, np.where(above, t - mx, 0))
    edge = np.where(below, mn, mx)
    sel = (below | above) & (gap >= 5) & (gap <= 40)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = sel & (edge <= 20); b = sel & (edge >= 60)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > cross_length_leading_digit.py
# name: cross_length_leading_digit
# description: Among sets whose examples are all one-digit, yes-rate on two-digit targets whose first digit equals some example's digit (35 after 3) minus two-digit targets whose first digit matches none; observed < null means people do not carry the leading-digit match across one- vs two-digit numbers as the model assumes (model over-produces this boost), observed > null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    onedig = (ex.max(axis=1) < 10).values
    lead = t.astype(str).str[0].astype(int).values
    match = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
    for c in ex.columns:
        v = ex[c].values
        match |= (v < 10) & (v == lead)
    sel = onedig & (t.values >= 10) & (t.values <= 99)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = sel & match; b = sel & ~match
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > even_vs_odd_set_parity_asymmetry.py
# name: even_vs_odd_set_parity_asymmetry
# description: (Yes-rate on even minus odd non-example targets in all-even sets of 2+ examples) minus (yes-rate on odd minus even non-example targets in all-odd sets of 2+ examples); observed > null means people abstract an "even numbers" rule more than an "odd numbers" rule, an asymmetry the model's symmetric parity similarity cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    k = ex.notna().sum(axis=1).values
    par = ex % 2
    alleven = ((par == 0) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1).values & (k >= 2)
    allodd = ((par == 1) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1).values & (k >= 2)
    isex = (ex.values == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    ev = t % 2 == 0
    def m(x):
        return r[x].mean() if x.sum() > 0 else np.nan
    de = m(alleven & ~isex & ev) - m(alleven & ~isex & ~ev)
    do = m(allodd & ~isex & ~ev) - m(allodd & ~isex & ev)
    v = de - do
    return float(v) if np.isfinite(v) else 0.0
EOF

# name: prime_set_prime_target_boost
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all prime, yes-rate on prime non-example targets minus odd non-prime targets (parity-matched control); observed > null means people infer a "prime numbers" concept that the model (no prime hypothesis) under-produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    primes = [n for n in range(2, 101) if all(n % p for p in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1))]
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    k = ex.notna().sum(axis=1).values
    allp = (ex.isin(primes) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1).values & (k >= 2)
    isex = (ex.values == t.values[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    tp = t.isin(primes).values
    odd = (t.values % 2 == 1)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = allp & ~isex & tp; b = allp & ~isex & ~tp & odd
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > single_example_breadth.py
# name: single_example_breadth
# description: Overall yes-rate on one-example sets minus the overall yes-rate on sets of 2+ examples; observed > null means people generalize from a single example more broadly, relative to multi-example sets, than the model does (model under-produces the size-principle drop from 1 to 2+ examples), observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    k = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.count(",").values + 1
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    if (k == 1).sum() == 0 or (k >= 2).sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[k == 1].mean() - r[k >= 2].mean())
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > factor_rule_odd_vs_even_g.py
# name: factor_rule_odd_vs_even_g
# description: Multiple-minus-non-multiple yes-rate gap (non-example targets) for sets whose GCD g is even and >= 4 minus the same gap for sets whose g is odd and >= 3; observed > null means people pick up "multiples of g" more readily for even g (4, 8, 12...) than odd g (3, 9...), which the model's log(g)-scaled rule does not capture (it over-predicts odd-g and under-predicts even-g rules).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    k = (ex > 0).sum(axis=1)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(ex, axis=1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    base = (k >= 2) & ~isex & (g >= 3)
    mult = (t % np.maximum(g, 1)) == 0
    def gap(s):
        a = s & mult; b = s & ~mult
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return np.nan
        return r[a].mean() - r[b].mean()
    v = gap(base & (g % 2 == 0)) - gap(base & (g % 2 == 1))
    return float(v) if np.isfinite(v) else 0.0
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > power_sequence_concept.py
# name: power_sequence_concept
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all powers of 2 or all perfect squares, yes-rate on non-example targets in that same family minus non-example targets outside it; observed > null means people infer "powers of 2" / "square numbers" concepts that the model (only multiples-of-g, final digit and factor similarity) under-produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    p2 = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]
    sq = [i * i for i in range(1, 11)]
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    k = ex.notna().sum(axis=1).values
    allp2 = (ex.isin(p2) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1).values & (k >= 2)
    allsq = (ex.isin(sq) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1).values & (k >= 2) & ~allp2
    isex = (ex.values == t.values[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    infam = np.where(allp2, t.isin(p2).values, t.isin(sq).values)
    s = (allp2 | allsq) & ~isex
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = s & infam; b = s & ~infam
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
EOF

| Statistic | What it probes in `leading_digit_string_similarity` | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| `set_level_yes_rate_dispersion` | Spread of yes-rates across sets. Earlier fits gave about 0.147 observed vs 0.116 predicted. | 0.147 |

| `cross_length_leading_digit` | Whether the all-or-none leading-digit match really carries from one-digit to two-digit numbers (3 → 35). This tests the incumbent's new mechanism directly. | +0.093 |
| `even_vs_odd_set_parity_asymmetry` | An "even numbers" rule stronger than any "odd numbers" rule. The model's parity similarity treats both the same. | +0.139 |
| `prime_set_prime_target_boost` | A "primes" concept, compared against odd non-prime targets so parity doesn't drive it. The model has no primes concept. | +0.087 |
| `single_example_breadth` | How much broader people generalize from one example than from two or more. | +0.100 |
| `factor_rule_odd_vs_even_g` | The "multiples of g" effect for even g (4, 8, …) minus odd g (3, 9, …). The model scales this rule only by log g. | −0.079 |
| `power_sequence_concept` | "Powers of 2" or "square numbers" concepts. Only a few sets qualify, so this one has little power. | +0.008 |

`factor_rule_odd_vs_even_g` came out negative, which is the opposite of what my earlier residual notes suggested. Its description states what each direction means, so the reading still holds once the null comparison comes in.
